Mathematical Problem
An 𝒏\bm{n}-label is a permutation of the numbers 1 through nn. For example, J=35214J=35214 is a 5-label and K=132K=132 is a 3-label. For a fixed positive integer pp, where p≤np\leq n, consider consecutive blocks of pp numbers in an nn-label. For example, when p=3p=3 and L=263415L=263415, the blocks are 263, 634, 341, and 415. We can associate to each of these blocks a pp-label that corresponds to the relative order of the numbers in that block. For L=263415L=263415, we get the following:

Moving from left to right in the nn-label, there are n−p+1n-p+1 such blocks, which means we obtain an (n−p+1)(n-p+1)-tuple of pp-labels. For L=263415L=263415, we get the 4-tuple (132,312,231,213)(132,312,231,213). We will call this (n−p+1)(n-p+1)-tuple the 𝒑\bm{p}-signature of LL (or signature, if pp is clear from the context) and denote it by Sp​[L]S_{p}[L]; the pp-labels in the signature are called windows. For L=263415L=263415, the windows are 132, 312, 231, and 213, and we write

More generally, we will call any (n−p+1)(n-p+1)-tuple of pp-labels a pp-signature, even if we do not know of an nn-label to which it corresponds (and even if no such label exists). A signature that occurs for exactly one nn-label is called unique, and a signature that doesn’t occur for any nn-labels is called impossible. A possible signature is one that occurs for at least one nn-label.
In this power question, you will be asked to analyze some of the properties of labels and signatures.
